identification.summary: DragonSpark is the name SentinelLABS (SentinelOne) gave to an activity cluster that used the open-source, Go-based SparkRAT against organizations in East Asia, staging tools from compromised servers in China and Taiwan [S1][S2][S3]. SentinelLABS described it as the first activity cluster in which SparkRAT was consistently used in attacks, while noting other adversaries also appear to use the tool [S3].
identification.notes: First-observed month (September 2022) comes from secondary coverage of the SentinelLABS report [S4]. Microsoft reported SparkRAT misuse in December 2022; SentinelLABS found no concrete link between that activity and DragonSpark, so the two should not be merged [S3]. One secondary source reports a shared C2 IP with Zegost infostealer activity; this is single-sourced and not a cluster merge [S2].

attribution.confidence: SentinelLABS assessed it as highly likely that a Chinese-speaking actor is behind the DragonSpark attacks [S1][S3].
attribution.basis: SentinelLABS based its assessment on the actor's tooling, including Chinese-developed open-source tools and use of the China Chopper webshell, and on compromised infrastructure in China and Taiwan [S3]. No state sponsor or government attribution was found in the sources reviewed; the sources describe the actor as Chinese-speaking only.

targeting.notes: Sources describe organizations in East Asia, with compromised networks in Taiwan, Hong Kong, China and Singapore belonging to gambling-related companies, art galleries, travel agencies and schools [S2][S4]. It is not clear from the sources whether these were end victims or only infrastructure used for staging; some staging servers belonged to legitimate businesses [S2]. Initial indicators were compromised web servers and internet-exposed MySQL database servers [S2].

capabilities.summary: SparkRAT is an open-source, multi-platform remote access tool written in Go that runs on Windows, Linux and macOS, communicates with its C2 over WebSocket and can update itself via the C2 [S1][S2][S3]. DragonSpark also used a custom loader (m6699.exe) that uses the Yaegi framework to interpret Go source code embedded in the binary at runtime, which hinders static analysis [S3][S4]. The actor used the China Chopper webshell and other Chinese-developed open-source tools including SharpToken and BadPotato (privilege escalation) and GoToHTTP (remote access) [S4]. Coverage also lists XZB-1248 and a shellcode loader among tools [S4].

campaigns.name: DragonSpark operations first observed
campaigns.summary: Operations attributed to the DragonSpark cluster were first observed in September 2022, using compromised web and MySQL servers for initial access and China Chopper webshells [S4][S2].

campaigns.name: Microsoft reporting on SparkRAT misuse (not linked to DragonSpark)
campaigns.summary: Microsoft reported in December 2022 that threat actors were increasingly using SparkRAT; SentinelLABS found no concrete link between that activity and DragonSpark [S3].

campaigns.name: SentinelLABS publishes DragonSpark report
campaigns.summary: SentinelLABS publicly described the cluster, its staging infrastructure in Taiwan, Hong Kong, China and Singapore, C2 servers in Hong Kong and the US, and the Yaegi-based loader [S1][S2][S4].

diamond.adversary: Chinese-speaking actor, assessed highly likely by SentinelLABS; no sponsor identified [S1][S3].
diamond.capability: SparkRAT, Yaegi-based Go source interpreting loader, China Chopper, SharpToken, BadPotato, GoToHTTP [S3][S4].
diamond.infrastructure: Staging on compromised servers in Taiwan, Hong Kong, China and Singapore (some belonging to legitimate businesses); C2 servers in Hong Kong and the US [S2][S4].
diamond.victim: Organizations in East Asia, including gambling-related companies, art galleries, travel agencies and schools [S2][S4].
diamond.technology: Internet-exposed web servers and MySQL databases; Windows, Linux and macOS endpoints via cross-platform Go tooling [S2][S3].

gaps: Primary SentinelLABS report could not be opened in this session (fetch failed); details rely on search-result summaries and secondary coverage.
Microsoft's December 2022 SparkRAT report was not located or read; overlap or non-overlap with DragonSpark rests on SentinelLABS statements as relayed by media [S3].
No sponsor, objective (espionage vs financial), or government attribution is established by the sources.
Activity after January 2023 not researched or found.
Zegost shared-C2 claim is single-sourced [S2]; ATT&CK group ID not assigned.
Sources S5 (The Record) and S6 (SC Media) removed: URLs not confirmed in fact-check searches.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Step 1-2: relevant environment is internet-facing web and MySQL servers and cross-platform endpoints in East Asian organizations [S2][S3]. Step 3 (adversary): a Chinese-speaking actor using open-source tooling, so capability is modest but evasive [S1][S3]. MLCOA (assessment): continued opportunistic compromise of exposed web/database servers with China Chopper then SparkRAT staging from compromised third-party hosts [S2]. MDCOA (assessment): use of the same cross-platform RAT and interpreted-Go loaders against Linux/macOS or other regional networks [S3]. Candidate indicators: China Chopper requests to web servers, Yaegi-embedded Go binaries, SparkRAT WebSocket C2 traffic, outbound connections to Hong Kong/US C2 [S3].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: share SparkRAT/Yaegi loader and China Chopper detections with partners operating in East Asia, noting reporting is vendor-sourced [S1][S3]. Authorities: any response beyond owned networks needs proper DODIN/DCO authority review; no government attribution exists to rely on. Mission assurance: harden and monitor internet-exposed web and MySQL servers and watch for compromised third-party hosts used for staging [S2]. Coordination: coordinate with vendor and allied partners given the Taiwan/Hong Kong/China/Singapore footprint [S2].
